## Charter

# CHARTER — Off-Peak Fare Capping at Riverton Transit Authority: A Briefing Note

## Deliverable
What: A briefing note to the Riverton Transit Authority (RTA) Board of
Directors evaluating whether RTA should adopt an off-peak fare cap, and
recommending how. Through-line: RTA should adopt an off-peak fare cap
through a phased, corridor-first pilot, because peer-agency evidence shows
off-peak capping grows ridership without a full-fare-equivalent revenue
loss, and RTA's own ridership and equity data show the riders most
underserved by its current all-day cap are exactly the riders concentrated
in the off-peak window.
Format: markdown, rendered last via the format skill
Total size: 4200w, 5items
(body sections only, B002-B006; the executive summary is front-matter.md and
the conclusion/recommendation is back-matter.md, written by hand in the seam
pass — see PLAN.md and WALKTHROUGH.md — and are not separately budgeted plan
units)

## Audience
The RTA Board of Directors and the General Manager's senior staff. They know
RTA's network and current fare structure well; they do not have the peer-
agency data, the fare-system technical constraints, or the equity office's
analysis in front of them, and this note is their first consolidated look at
all three together ahead of a vote on whether to direct staff to proceed.

## Voice & register
Third person, board-briefing register: precise, plain, comfortable citing
figures, and willing to name a tradeoff without hiding it. No first person,
no rhetorical questions, and no recommendation stated as settled until the
conclusion — body sections lay out evidence and tradeoffs, not verdicts.

## Non-negotiables
1. Every ridership, revenue, cost, or date figure carries a [S#] source tag
   traceable to a file in Sources of truth.
2. The terminology lock is followed exactly; no synonyms for locked terms.
3. The implementation options section presents at least two options as
   options the Board could choose among, never as a decision already made.
4. Equity implications for low-income riders are addressed as their own
   subject, not folded into a general accessibility statement.
5. No section before the conclusion states outright that RTA should adopt
   an off-peak cap; sections build the evidence, the conclusion states the
   recommendation.

   catalog lists all five sources.
2. The section on RTA's own ridership data ties the existing all-day cap's

3. The equity section states at least one quantified finding from [S4]
   about who is underserved by the current cap.
4. The operational/technical feasibility section distinguishes the
   real-time and interim batch-credit options from [S3], with their
   respective costs and timelines.
5. The implementation options section presents at least two phasing options
   without declaring either one the Board's decision.
6. The finished piece (final.md, body plus front matter and back matter) is

   conclusion's recommendation is supported by evidence already stated in

## Established facts
- Peer agencies [S1], now stated in full in Section 1: Meridian +11%
  off-peak boardings/+4% off-peak revenue/$340k/7mo (system-wide, 2023);
  Cedar Falls +18% enrolled off-peak boardings/-0.6% system revenue/$95k
  (enrolled-only, 2022); Ashford +7% corridor off-peak boardings/34% rider
  awareness by month 6/$110k/5mo (single-corridor pilot, 2024-25, board
  later voted system-wide expansion for 2027).
- Cross-agency: ridership gains were mostly marginal trips, not
  peak-fare substitution; no crowding/service-cost increase in any of the
  three; Meridian's union got 6 weeks' notice, no labor dispute reported.
- RTA [S2, not yet stated in body]: 21.4M FY2026 boardings; all-day cap
  since 2019 (2 taps/day, time-blind); off-peak = 4.7M boardings (22%),
  $5.7M revenue; 62% of off-peak boardings get no cap benefit; off-peak
  occupancy 34% vs 78% AM peak.

## Interfaces/terms now defined
- "off-peak fare cap" (Section 1) — pays off after fewer taps, only for
  taps inside the off-peak window; distinct from RTA's all-day, time-blind
  cap.

### sources/riverton-ridership-data.md

# Data memo — RTA ridership and fare revenue by time period

Prepared by RTA Planning & Scheduling from the FY2026 automated fare
collection (AFC) extract and the FY2026 operating budget. Figures cover
Riverton Transit Authority's fixed-route bus and light-rail network only;
paratransit (RTA Access) is reported separately in the stakeholder notes.

## System totals, FY2026

RTA recorded 21.4 million unweighted boardings in FY2026, up 1.8% from
FY2025. Fixed-route fare revenue was $28.6 million. RTA's existing fare
product is a single all-day cap: a rider pays full fare for their first 2
taps in a service day (6:00 a.m.-11:59 p.m.) and rides free the rest of that
day, regardless of when those first 2 taps occur. This all-day cap has been
in place since 2019 and is not time-of-day differentiated.

## Boardings and revenue by day-part

RTA's AFC system buckets boardings into three day-parts: AM peak (6:00-9:30
a.m.), midday/PM peak combined as "daytime" (9:30 a.m.-6:30 p.m., which
includes the 4:00-6:30 p.m. PM peak), and off-peak (6:30 p.m.-11:59 p.m. plus
all weekend hours). For FY2026:

- AM peak: 6.2 million boardings (29% of system total), $9.1 million revenue.
- Daytime (including PM peak): 10.5 million boardings (49% of system total),
  $13.8 million revenue.
- Off-peak (evenings and weekends): 4.7 million boardings (22% of system
  total), $5.7 million revenue.

Average fare revenue per boarding is therefore highest in AM peak ($1.47)
and lowest off-peak ($1.21), consistent with the existing all-day cap: a
rider who taps twice in the morning rush already rides free for the rest of
the day, including any off-peak trips, so off-peak boardings by cap-covered
riders generate no incremental revenue at all. RTA Planning estimates 38% of
off-peak boardings are made by riders who already reached the all-day cap
earlier that same day; the remaining 62% are riders making an off-peak-only
trip (a single fare, no cap benefit) or a second trip on a day when their
first trip was also off-peak.

## Growth and capacity

Off-peak ridership grew 3.1% year over year, faster than the 1.8% system
average, driven mostly by evening service on the two light-rail lines. RTA's
fleet utilization data shows off-peak trips run at 34% average seat
occupancy system-wide, compared with 78% in AM peak and 71% in PM peak — RTA
has substantial unused off-peak capacity on nearly every route. No route in
the FY2026 schedule is capacity-constrained off-peak.

## Prior fare-change history

RTA's board last changed the base fare in 2021 (a $0.15 increase) and
introduced the current all-day cap in 2019. Both changes went through a
90-day public comment period under RTA's fare-change policy. RTA has not
previously implemented a fare product differentiated by time of day; the
all-day cap is uniform regardless of when a rider's first two taps occur.
